analysis.one_liner: Makes it a felony, with prison time, for employers whose willful safety violations kill workers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in two House committees and their subcommittees until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the law in 2005, an employer who willfully violated safety rules and a worker died faced at most six months in jail and a small fine. This bill would have turned that into a felony carrying up to ten years in prison for a first offense and twenty for a repeat offense, with fines set under the standard federal criminal schedule. It also raised penalties for failing to report a workplace death and for tipping off an employer before an inspection. It was introduced by a single New York Democrat, gathered no cosponsors, and died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in dangerous jobs — construction, manufacturing, meatpacking, and similar industries — whose deaths from willful safety violations would carry real criminal consequences for their employers for the first time. Stronger penalties can also deter violations before a death happens.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers in hazardous jobs and their families

how_it_helps.text: For a willful safety violation that kills a worker, the bill replaces the old maximum of a $10,000 fine and six months in jail with fines under the standard federal criminal schedule and up to ten years in prison [S3].
For a repeat conviction, the maximum prison term rises from one year to twenty years [S3].

Failing to report a workplace death or serious injury would carry up to two years in prison instead of six months, and giving advance notice of an OSHA inspection would carry up to one year instead of six months [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers — especially those in industries with high fatality rates — who would face felony prosecution, multi-year prison terms, and much larger fines when a willful safety violation kills a worker.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers with safety violations that kill workers

drawbacks.text: The bill raises penalties sharply but does not add inspectors or enforcement resources, so critics could argue that prison terms deter only when violations are actually detected — and OSHA inspections were already rare [S3].

Business groups generally oppose criminalizing workplace deaths on the grounds that employers already face civil liability and that felony exposure for accidents can make managers defensive about cooperating with investigations; that objection does not appear in the provided record.

Doubling the maximum for repeat offenses to twenty years is a stiff sentence for a regulatory violation, even one that kills, and an honest supporter would acknowledge that prosecutors would use this power selectively.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change is well-targeted: it keeps the existing requirement that the violation be willful and a death result, and simply stops treating a preventable workplace death as a minor misdemeanor. The main weakness is that penalties without more inspections may rarely be triggered, so the practical benefit depends on prosecutors actually using the new felony authority.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and then to subcommittees, and neither ever took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Major Owens introduced the bill on April 28, 2005 [S1].
The Speaker referred it to both the Education and the Workforce Committee and the Judiciary Committee [S5].
It was sent to the Workforce Protections Subcommittee on May 20 and to the Crime subcommittee on June 6, 2005, and no further action was ever recorded [S5].
No other member cosponsored the bill [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers in hazardous industries, who avoided new felony prison exposure for willful safety violations that kill workers, kept in place the old six-month maximum.

sides.party_line_note: No floor vote was ever held and no member of either party cosponsored the bill, so opposition never had to take a position on the record.

industries.industry: Employers in hazardous industries (construction, manufacturing, meatpacking)
industries.note: The bill would have exposed their officers and managers to felony prosecution, up to ten or twenty years in prison, and much larger fines when a willful safety violation kills a worker. Their interest in the bill's failure ran directly against workers' safety.
